Internal Design Document

Nochore Harness Layer

One agent. One pipeline. Graduated intelligence.

The Harness Layer is a typed pipeline runner that executes the same eight-step sequence for every agent — from a simple invoice processor to a complex ad spend optimizer. Simpler agents degenerate naturally: fewer skills means trivial scope resolution, no memory means empty context, auto-approve policy means a passthrough gate. The pipeline doesn't branch for complexity; it absorbs it.

The user sees one concept: an agent that does a job. The runtime decides how much intelligence each step requires. The contracts are locked; the execution model evolves.

Status Design Complete
Timeline 12 weeks / 6 phases
Tasks 22 implementation tasks
Date March 2026
The Architectural Bet
We bet on typed contracts with flexible runtime rather than a fixed execution model. Lock down: Skill interfaces, policy schema, memory format, action contracts — stable because they model real domain boundaries. Keep flexible: How scope resolution works, whether skills use deterministic code or LLM reasoning, how the planner synthesizes. Today's ratio might be 70% deterministic / 30% LLM. In two years it could be 20/80. The user never notices the shift.

System Architecture

Three layers: the frontend users interact with, the harness where agents live, and the external services that provide data and actions.

Figure 1 — System architecture showing the three-layer separation between frontend, harness, and external services.

Three Layers

  • Frontend (TanStack Start) — React 19 application with five agent tabs: Monitor, Feed, Chat, Memory, Settings. Server functions import directly from the harness package.
  • Harness Layer — The typed pipeline runner. Contains contracts, pipeline orchestration (trigger.dev), skill system, policy engine, memory store, and chat handler (Vercel AI SDK streamText). Lives in packages/harness/.
  • External Services — Google Ads, Meta Ads, GA4, Search Console via Composio SDK. LLM providers via Vercel AI SDK (provider-agnostic). SQLite for persistence.

What This Is NOT

  • Not a workflow engine. There are no user-visible "steps" or "sequences." The pipeline is internal.
  • Not an agent framework. We don't expose orchestration primitives. Each agent is self-contained.
  • Not an AI wrapper. Most of the pipeline is deterministic code. LLM reasoning is injected at specific, bounded seams.

The Pipeline

Every agent run — triggered by schedule, webhook, chat command, or manual invocation — walks this eight-step pipeline. Each step is a trigger.dev task with built-in retry, tracing, and idempotency.

Figure 2 — The 8-step agent run pipeline with LLM injection points and data flow between steps.

The Eight Steps

  1. Trigger — Cron, webhook, chat command, or manual invocation. Always deterministic.
  2. Scope Resolution — Resolve which skills matter for this run. Static config for simple agents, LLM-decided for complex ones. Consults memory (lessons) for context.
  3. Fetch — Collect data types from selected skills, resolve to tools via Connection Manager, fetch in parallel. Fully deterministic.
  4. Analyze — Run skills in parallel. Each skill is either a structured LLM call (system prompt + data) or a deterministic function. The skill contract is the same either way.
  5. Plan — Synthesize all skill outputs + intent + memory into concrete ActionProposals. Single LLM call for cross-skill reasoning. Passthrough if only one obvious action.
  6. Policy Gate — Deterministic rule engine. No LLM. Ever. Per-action overrides, threshold tiers, operational constraints, global switch. Strictest result wins.
  7. Execute — Tool calls via Connection Manager. Only for auto-approved and user-approved actions. Deterministic.
  8. Memory Write — Layer 1: Event log (always, append-only). Layer 2: Lesson distillation (periodic LLM summarization).

LLM Injection Points

LLM reasoning is bounded to specific steps. The safety-critical path (Policy Gate, Execute) is always deterministic.

Step Deterministic? LLM? Notes
1. Trigger Always Never Cron, webhook, or explicit invocation
2. Scope Resolution Can be Can be Static config for simple agents, LLM for complex
3. Fetch Always Never API calls via Connection Manager
4. Analyze Can be Can be Skill contract is the same regardless
5. Plan — Usually Passthrough for single-action agents
6. Policy Gate Always Never Safety path is always deterministic
7. Execute Always Never Tool calls, not reasoning
8. Memory Write Events: always Lessons: LLM Event log is mechanical; lesson distillation uses LLM
End-to-End Example: Ad Spend Guardian daily at 9am
4 LLM calls, ~10K input tokens, ~1.8K output tokens. Estimated cost: ~$0.04 (Sonnet pricing). Duration: ~8 seconds. The pipeline found 5 wasteful search terms burning $340/day, auto-approved adding 3 negative keywords, and queued a 15% budget reduction for human approval.

Human-in-the-Loop

The policy gate produces three outcomes: AUTO (execute immediately), QUEUE (needs human approval), and BLOCK (rejected with reason). The checkpoint/resume pattern handles the approval flow with zero idle compute cost.

Figure 3 — Human-in-the-loop approval flow using trigger.dev checkpoint/resume pattern.

The Checkpoint/Resume Pattern

When an action needs user approval, trigger.dev checkpoints the entire run state, suspends the task (releasing compute), and resumes exactly where it left off when the user approves — hours or days later. No idle cost. No polling.

How It Works

  1. Policy gate classifies a proposal as needs_review
  2. Pipeline stores the pending proposal in the database
  3. trigger.dev task calls wait.forEvent() — the task suspends, compute is released
  4. Frontend shows the pending action in the Feed with Approve/Reject buttons
  5. User clicks Approve — frontend POSTs to trigger.dev to resume the event
  6. Task resumes exactly at the checkpoint, executes the approved action
  7. Auto-expires after 7 days if no decision is made
Why This Matters
Traditional approaches use polling loops or webhook callbacks with manual state reconstruction. The checkpoint/resume pattern preserves the full execution context across the wait boundary — no serialization, no state machines, no custom queue infrastructure.

Graduated Intelligence

The same pipeline handles vastly different agents. Complexity is not a mode — it's a consequence of configuration. Simple agents degenerate naturally through the pipeline.

Figure 4 — How the same pipeline handles simple vs complex agents through natural degeneration.

Side-by-Side Comparison

Simple Agent (Invoice Processor)

  • 1 skill (extract_invoice)
  • Scope: static (always run the one skill)
  • Data sources: 1 (email attachment)
  • Analyze: deterministic extraction
  • Plan: passthrough (one action)
  • Policy: auto-approve all
  • Memory: event log only
  • LLM calls per run: 0–1

Complex Agent (Ad Spend Optimizer)

  • 5 skills (search terms, budget, QS, trends, composition)
  • Scope: LLM-decided (picks relevant skills per run)
  • Data sources: 4 (Google Ads, Meta, GA4, Search Console)
  • Analyze: structured LLM reasoning
  • Plan: cross-skill LLM planner
  • Policy: threshold tiers + approval gates
  • Memory: events + distilled lessons
  • LLM calls per run: 5–7

The pipeline doesn't branch. It absorbs complexity. A simple agent is just a complex agent where most steps are trivial passthroughs.

Contracts

These four interfaces are locked down because they model real domain boundaries proven in the legacy CLI. They change rarely and with care.

Skill

A skill is EITHER a structured LLM call (systemPrompt + output schema) OR a deterministic function (compute). The harness doesn't care which — the contract is: data in, typed output out.

interface Skill<TOutput> {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  description: string;

  // What data this skill needs — NOT which tool provides it
  consumes: DataType[];

  // Typed output schema
  produces: Schema<TOutput>;

  // Domain expertise (for LLM-powered skills)
  systemPrompt?: string;

  // OR deterministic implementation
  compute?: (data: SkillData) => TOutput;

  // Optional domain knowledge (client-specific context)
  knowledge?: string;
}

ActionProposal

A concrete, typed proposal for an action the agent wants to take. Every proposal has a confidence score, a human-readable reason, and an idempotency key to prevent duplicate execution.

interface ActionProposal {
  id: string;
  action: string;           // e.g., "add_negative_keyword"
  toolCategory: string;     // e.g., "google_ads"
  args: Record<string, unknown>;
  reason: string;           // Human-readable explanation
  confidence: number;       // 0–1
  skillSource: string;      // Which skill generated this
  reversible: boolean;
  idempotencyKey: string;   // Prevents duplicate execution
}

PolicyRule

Policy evaluation is a pure function chain. The strictest result wins. No LLM involvement — ever. The safety path must be auditable and predictable.

interface PolicyRule {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  priority: number;  // Lower = evaluated first

  evaluate(
    proposal: ActionProposal,
    context: PolicyContext
  ): PolicyDecision;
}

type PolicyDecision =
  | { result: "approved";     reason: string }
  | { result: "needs_review"; reason: string }
  | { result: "blocked";      reason: string };

MemoryStore

Two-layer memory: an append-only event log for lossless truth, and distilled lessons for efficient context injection. Events are mechanical; lesson distillation uses LLM.

interface MemoryStore {
  // Layer 1: Event log (append-only, never edited)
  appendEvent(event: AgentEvent): void;
  queryEvents(filter: EventFilter): AgentEvent[];

  // Layer 2: Distilled lessons (periodic LLM summarization)
  getLessons(scope?: string): Lesson[];
  distillLessons(recentEvents: AgentEvent[]): Lesson[];
}

interface Lesson {
  id: string;
  content: string;          // Human-readable lesson
  scope: string;            // Which skill/domain this applies to
  confidence: "high" | "medium" | "low";
  sourceEventIds: string[]; // Traceability
  createdAt: Date;
  expiresAt?: Date;         // Some lessons are time-bound
}

Tech Stack

Every technology choice is deliberate. We optimize for zero infrastructure at launch, provider independence, and the ability to evolve the execution model without changing contracts.

Layer Technology Rationale
LLM Communication Vercel AI SDK Provider-agnostic. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Bedrock through one interface. No lock-in.
Chat Agent Vercel AI SDK streamText with tool calling, stateless per-request. Powers interactive Chat tab.
Pipeline Orchestration trigger.dev v3 Durable execution with retry, checkpoint/resume, cron triggers, OpenTelemetry, idempotency.
Schema Validation Zod Zod for all validation — skill outputs, tool parameters, type contracts. Unified schema language.
Database SQLite via Drizzle ORM Single-file database per project. Zero infrastructure. Events, lessons, agent configs.
Frontend TanStack Start React 19, Vite 7. Server functions import harness directly. Already exists in apps/web/.
Integrations Composio SDK OAuth flows, 500+ app connections. Wrapped by our Connection Manager.
Sandbox (future) E2B Firecracker microVM sandboxes for marketplace skills. Not needed for MVP.

What trigger.dev Replaces

trigger.dev provides critical infrastructure we would otherwise build from scratch.

Need Without trigger.dev With trigger.dev
Scheduling node-cron (in-process, no persistence) Built-in cron triggers (durable)
Orchestration Custom runner (no crash recovery) Task + subtask orchestration with CRIU checkpointing
Retry Logic Manual implementation Automatic retry with configurable exponential backoff
Human-in-the-Loop Custom approval queue + polling Checkpoint/suspend then resume (zero idle cost)
Observability Custom logging OpenTelemetry traces, auto-correlated across subtasks
Idempotency Custom dedup logic Built-in idempotency keys
Parallel Execution Promise.all (fragile) batchTriggerAndWait (durable, monitored)

Two Runtimes

The harness has two execution modes that share the same contracts and skill system.

Mode 1: Triggered Run

  • trigger.dev task (durable orchestration)
  • Steps 2–8 as sequential subtasks
  • AI SDK for LLM calls at seams
  • Checkpoint/resume for approval
  • Built-in retry, tracing, idempotency

Mode 2: Chat

  • Vercel AI SDK streamText (stateless per-request)
  • User msg → LLM reasons → calls tools
  • 10 tools (5 domain + 4 workspace-scoped)
  • Can trigger pipeline steps from chat
  • Same policy gate applies

Chat Mode

Chat mode shares the pipeline but is driven by conversation. The agent is the same entity in interactive mode — not a separate system. Uses Vercel AI SDK streamText with ten registered Nochore tools.

The 5 Registered Tools

Tool Triggered By What It Does
run_analysis "Run a fresh analysis on Campaign X" Creates a scoped TriggerEvent, invokes pipeline steps 2–8, returns summary to LLM
get_insights "What did you find last time?" Queries recent skill outputs from memory, returns structured insights
apply_action "Go ahead and add those negatives" Loads pending proposals, runs through same policy gate, executes approved ones
query_memory "What have you learned about this client?" Searches events and distilled lessons, returns relevant history
explain_decision "Why did you block that budget change?" Traces a specific decision back through policy rules and skill outputs

Chat Flow

User message
→
Chat LLM reasons
→
Calls tool (or responds)
→
Tool executes
→
LLM presents results

Chat-triggered runs are scoped. "Check Campaign X" narrows the pipeline to Campaign X only. The same policy gate applies — chat cannot bypass safety.

Progressive Evolution
As LLMs improve, Mode 1 (trigger.dev tasks) can gradually shift toward Mode 2 (AI SDK agentic loop). Pipeline steps become tools the LLM calls dynamically. The contracts stay the same. The user sees the same Feed, the same Monitor, the same Chat.

Implementation Roadmap

6 phases, 22 tasks, 12 weeks. Each phase builds on the previous. Parallelizable tasks are identified in the dependency graph.

Phase 1: Foundation

Week 1–2
  • Task 1: Monorepo package scaffold
  • Task 2: Type contracts — Skill, Action, Policy
  • Task 3: Type contracts — Memory, AgentConfig, Run
  • Task 4: Database schema (Drizzle + SQLite)

Phase 2: Core Engine

Week 3–4
  • Task 5: Memory store (event log + lessons)
  • Task 6: Policy engine with 4 built-in rules
  • Task 7: Skill registry & executor
  • Task 8: First built-in skill (Search Terms)

Phase 3: Pipeline

Week 5–6
  • Task 9: trigger.dev setup
  • Task 10: Pipeline steps (scope, fetch, analyze)
  • Task 11: Pipeline steps (plan, policy, execute, memory)
  • Task 12: Pipeline orchestrator (agent-run task)
  • Task 13: Trigger system (cron + webhook)

Phase 4: Chat + Connections

Week 7–8
  • Task 14: Connection Manager (stub)
  • Task 15: Chat handler (AI SDK streamText + 10 tools)

Phase 5: Frontend Integration

Week 9–10
  • Task 16: Server functions (agents, runs, chat, approvals)
  • Task 17: Feed component (decision log + approval cards)
  • Task 18: Chat component (AI SDK useChat hook)

Phase 6: First Live Agent

Week 11–12
  • Task 19: Remaining 6 built-in skills
  • Task 20: Composio integration (real Google Ads)
  • Task 21: "Ad Spend Guardian" — first live agent
  • Task 22: Lesson distillation (periodic LLM summarization)

Milestones

Design Decisions Log

Every architectural decision, the choice made, and the reasoning behind it. These decisions are the foundation of the system.

Decision Choice Rationale
Execution model Hybrid: event-driven + chat UX has both Monitor (event results) and Chat tabs
Skill routing LLM-decided (complex) or static (simple) Agents pursue objectives, not follow scripts
Data fetching Eager: fetch all, then analyze Clean separation; fetch is deterministic and parallelizable
Skill runtime Structured LLM call OR deterministic function Same contract, flexible implementation
Planning Unified planner (cross-skill LLM reasoning) One place for cross-skill synthesis
Policy gate Deterministic rule engine, no LLM ever Safety path must be auditable and predictable
Memory Event log (append-only) + distilled lessons Lossless truth + efficient context injection
Chat scope Can trigger pipeline steps Natural interaction without bypassing safety
Architecture pattern Pattern 3 surface + Pattern 4 internals One agent per job (simple UX), flexible runtime (evolves)
Workflow vs agent No separate concept Pipeline degenerates naturally for simple tasks
GTM Vertical-first: ad spend management Ship the product, build the platform underneath
Agent setup Platform feature first, agent later Ship smart form for MVP; graduate to learning agent at 50+ setups
Pipeline orchestration trigger.dev v3 Durable execution, retry, checkpoint/resume, OpenTelemetry, idempotency
LLM SDK Vercel AI SDK (provider-agnostic, Zod-native) Anthropic, OpenAI, Google through one interface. No lock-in.
Chat runtime Vercel AI SDK streamText with tool calling for interactive Chat tab
Sandbox (future) E2B Marketplace skills run in isolated Firecracker microVMs. Not needed for MVP.

Aspect 2026 Q2 (MVP) 2026 Q4 2027+

Policy 4 built-in rules User-configurable thresholds via UI Same engine, richer rules
